narrative:
Short impact summary

This scholarly book has established clear academic uptake, with 40 citations in OpenAlex and field-normalized standing in the top 10% for its year. Its influence is concentrated within archaeology, archaeometric analysis, and ancient materials research, and it was supported by European Research Council funding.

Full narrative

Glass Making in the Greco-Roman World: Results of the ARCHGLASS project has generated a strong scholarly response for a specialized monograph published by Leuven University Press in the Studies in Archaeological Sciences series. The record shows 40 citations, and its percentile position places it among the top 10% most-cited works in its field and publication year. That pattern indicates sustained use by researchers working on ancient glass, archaeological science, and the study of material production in the Mediterranean world.

The citing literature suggests that the book’s most visible contribution lies in the methods and questions it introduced around raw-material procurement and the geochemical study of glass production. Citations appear most often in archaeology and archaeometric venues, especially in journals such as the Journal of Archaeological Science, and they cluster around cultural heritage materials analysis, building materials and conservation, and historical-economic approaches to trade. This points to a work that is not only read within classical archaeology but is also used as a reference in broader materials-focused research.

The citation landscape is international and institutionally varied, with uptake across universities, museums, research institutes, and government-linked settings. The record also shows continuing use in recent years, including 2024 citations, which indicates that the book remains relevant to current research on ancient glass and related analytical methods. Its open-access availability through repository records may have further supported discovery and reuse, although the available evidence here is best read as scholarly visibility rather than direct proof of access effects.

Overall, the book’s impact is best described as durable scholarly influence within archaeology and archaeometry. The combination of a substantial citation count, top-decile percentile standing, and a citation profile centered on technical and historical studies of ancient materials shows that the ARCHGLASS project has helped shape how researchers investigate glass production, trade, and raw-material sourcing in the Greco-Roman world.
